# **Welcome to Project Julius**

| Before You Begin Read through every item on this page carefully. Working through everything will take time, but it is the most important time you will spend on this project. This is rare, specialized research, and only a small number of people in the world have both the expertise and the opportunity to do it. You’re one of them. We’re thrilled to have you onboard\!  |
| :---- |

## **Project Overview**

Project Julius is a unique opportunity to take AI agents out of the chat interface and into real professional environments, where they produce actual file outputs, interact with real tools, and complete the type of work you do every day.

AI models have become capable thought partners — they’re able to search the web, write code, and synthesize information at a high level. But being a strong thought partner isn't the same as doing the job. The harder frontier is whether a model can operate as an *agent*: plan across many steps, act inside real software and files, and deliver work a domain expert would actually accept.

That's the gap Project Julius is built to test. We recreate realistic work environments — "worlds" — and write challenging, multi-step tasks inside them, so we can measure where today's best models still fall short of a professional's standard. Your expertise is what makes that judgment possible.

## **Our Core Mission**

| Expert Experience Expert experience is top priority for this project and we want all experts to feel they are on the best project at Mercor. We will work to make the best systems, processes, staff, and guidelines to make this happen. | Quality Data This project pushes the boundaries of AI capability. We prioritize quality data and thoughtful work over data that is incorrect or low-effort. The work of this project will directly impact how systems behave and this project's shared responsibility to align models correctly. | Pushing the Frontier We want experts on this project to understand they are at the frontier and contribute in their specialized fields. We encourage all experts to ask thoughtful questions on edge cases, new research, or clarifications that might apply specifically to their domain. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

## **Workstreams**

The project is divided into two workstreams: World Building and Task Writing. In Project Julius, each expert owns a world end-to-end — these are not separate roles handed off between people. This sequencing matters: because you built the world yourself, you know exactly where its complexity lives, which makes for richer, more realistic tasks.

| World Building World Building creates simulated environments that mirror the file systems and apps professionals use every day. The work includes populating folders with artifacts. These artifacts will differ by domain, but they may include public data sets, contracts, financial analyses, meeting notes, presentations, and research. They should contain everything a real team folder would contain. World builders also generate synthetic data to seed databases such as QuickBooks, ADP Payroll, and Workday. Video walkthrough: [Setting up Agents Playground Golden Trajectories](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_e8GpVD4lWAbKbR-HMrlqLheZJ7xYAHm/view?usp=sharing) covers configuring golden trajectories in the Agents Playground as you build your world. | Task Writing Once their world is built, experts design realistic, multi-step tasks within it, based on how work actually gets done and how an LLM should execute it. Tasks may involve searching for information, running calculations, creating documents, updating databases, analyzing data, or coordinating multiple actions in sequence. A given task should take an industry expert at least 3-8 hours to execute unassisted by an AI agent. Tasks are designed at the frontier of the given domain to push AI models to the limits of their reasoning and deep research capabilities. Video walkthrough: [How to Capture Golden Agent Trajectories](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1NzM5YuEMmUaaKNUqWPd2hFAOVLsDTW3b/view?usp=sharing) shows how to record golden agent trajectories for your tasks. |
| :---- | :---- |

## **Project Expectations**

The following summarizes what we expect from you as a contributor on Project Julius.

| Minimum Activity | All experts must check in on Slack most days to see the latest updates. Because each expert owns a world end-to-end — building it, then writing tasks in it — the minimum world building commitment is 30 hours a week. Task writing has a minimum commitment of 20 hours a week. This project’s tasks take many hours with guidelines that may change.  Staying in touch on the latest and frequently contributing helps your work go smoothly. Notify an EPM or domain lead in advance if you can't meet this in a given week. Repeated misses may put your contract at risk. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Quality and Consistency** | Deliver clear, accurate, and well-supported work across every task and workstream. |
| **Onboarding Timeline** | Complete onboarding within 48 hours of becoming active. Your spec creation should be submitted within 24 hours of getting access to your domain. Feedback loops start early and you improve with each iteration\! |
| **Engagement and Community** | Stay responsive in Slack and within task interfaces. Prompt communication keeps workflows smooth and supports coordination between writers, reviewers, and leads.  **Treat all experts and staff with respect; we are one team.** |
| **Efficiency** | Work efficiently. Please ensure that you spend the necessary time to complete the quality needed, but do not sit idly on tasks. We expect \~10 hours per task (including all review and revision cycles). Submission means a task sent for review. Completion means a task that has passed our quality standards. |

| When Logging Time In Insightful, Select The Timer That Matches Your Current Phase Project Julius \- World Building, if you are actively building or refining your world. Project Julius \- Task Writing, if you are writing tasks within your world. Hours, Caps and Scheduling Your total hours across all active hourly projects must not exceed 80 hours per week. When you first join you start with a limited hour cap during onboarding; once you submit your plan creation that cap is raised. The pay period runs Saturday at 12:00 AM IST through Friday at 11:59 PM IST. A Thursday evening in the Americas can already be Friday in IST, so plan logging near the boundary carefully. What counts as paid time: in-scope task and world-building work, Mercor webinars, and approved coordination meetings or office hours while you are actively engaged. What does not count: idle time, off-scope or unrelated activity, policy violations, and spam. Scheduling is flexible; the cap is weekly, not daily, so you can work in whatever chunks suit you. For time off, contact your point of contact through Slack or email; requests are handled case by case. See [https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/time-tracking-pay](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/time-tracking-pay)  |
| :---- |

# **Quick Start Guide**

You're working at the frontier of AI, testing and improving models on highly complex, long-horizon tasks. The full instruction guide is long, so this guide exists to get you oriented, set up, and confident before you claim your first task. 

## **Day 1 Checklist**

Get these things done before you claim your first task. The most common onboarding issue is logging in with the wrong email or browser session, so use a private or incognito window for Mercor resources and confirm your @mercor.expert email is the active account.

| Mercor Account Support  Have questions about payments, accounts, Okta, or something else? Mercor maintains centralized talent docs that might be useful to you\! What is Mercor Mercor is a talent marketplace that connects you (the contractor) with companies that need expert work. Mercor handles your contract, onboarding, time tracking, and payments, so you can focus on the work itself. The company you support on this project relies on Mercor to vet experts, run the workflow, and pay you on a predictable schedule. PaymentPayouts run every Wednesday for the prior pay period, paid through Stripe (Wise where Stripe is unavailable in your country). See https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/time-tracking-pay Time tracking: hourly work is tracked through Insightful (the desktop app is branded Workpuls). See [https://talent.docs.mercor.com/how-to/use-insightful](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/how-to/use-insightful) Referrals You can refer other experts from the Referrals tab in your Mercor dashboard. See [https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/referrals](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/referrals) Social Media You may mention that you work with Mercor using only information that is already public, and you must keep all project details confidential under your CIIA. You are an independent contractor, not a Mercor employee. See [https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/social-media](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/social-media) Taxes You complete a W-9 (US persons) or W-8BEN (non-US persons) during onboarding. See [https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/taxes-work-authorization](https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/taxes-work-authorization) Payment Schedule and Disputes Payouts run on Wednesdays for the previous pay period and are processed by the end of Wednesday (PST), through Stripe as the primary method and Wise where Stripe is unavailable in your country. Your first payout may sit on a 7-day Stripe hold. The pay period runs Saturday at 12:00 AM IST through Friday at 11:59 PM IST. Note that a Thursday evening in the Americas can already be Friday in IST, which is the last day of the period. Common reasons a payout is missed: Stripe or Wise details are out of date, your background check is still pending, or there is a normal bank delay. Deductions can be triggered by idle timer activity, activity unrelated to your scope, off-scope work, duplicate or double tracking, an AI-policy violation, or spam. Every deduction is reviewed by a human and is not automated. If you believe a deduction is wrong, reply to the deduction email within the same pay period in which it was issued. Contracts on the project end on the same date unless your individual contract is extended. Completion badges are finalized once either the project itself officially ends or your individual contract for the project has ended, whichever comes first. Before any deadline, submit your outstanding hours, finish your deliverables, and keep your Stripe or Wise payout details current. ## **Ground Rules**

These are non-negotiable. Violating any of these will result in removal from the project.

| No Sensitive Content Do not write or request NSFW content, personally identifiable information (PII), or anything harmful, dangerous, or illegal. If a task prompt seems to ask for it, flag it in your domain channel and do not proceed. |
| :---- |

| Confidentiality Do not discuss the project, the models, or any project data outside designated Slack channels. Do not share screenshots, data, or results externally. Mentioning Mercor publicly is fine using only information that is already public; no project specifics. |
| :---- |

| Treating Others with Respect Expert experience is \#1 on this project, as a result we expect *all experts* to treat each other with respect. Our goal is to be the best project and malicious behavior or attitudes will not be tolerated. |
| :---- |

## **Project Norms and Reminders**

A handful of habits that make life easier for you and the team.

| What We Expect From You Check Slack at least once a day, even on days you are not working. A few minutes to review announcements keeps you in the loop. Commitment of 20 hours per week, in whatever chunks work for you. Folks below that tend to miss details and end up with rework. If you will be off for a stretch, give your lead a heads up.  Only log active hours. If you are sitting idly waiting for something (a trajectory run, etc.), clock out and take a break. Only log time when you are actively working on a task or on a call with us. Inactive or unresponsive experts will be removed from this project frequently.  Post in open channels, not DMs. Faster answers, and chances are someone else has the same question. Stay on task when tasking. Clock out for breaks. Manage timers carefully so we can project capacity and put support where it is needed. |
| :---- |

# **Glossary**

| Reference as you go\! This is a complicated project, but here is a quick list of terms you might see thrown around\! Reference below as you move through the instructions\! |
| :---- |

| 1\. The Project |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Project Julius** | Mercor's frontier research project building self-contained simulated professional environments and tasks that challenge AI agents to do real expert work. |
| **Frontier-class project** | Mercor's internal classification for projects that push the boundary of what current AI models can do. Julius is one. The bar for engagement and quality is higher than typical annotation work, and the volume of writers globally working on this style of data is small. |
| **2\. Core AI Agent vocabulary** |  |
| **Agent** | An AI system that takes actions in an environment to complete a task. Different from a chatbot in that it operates in a loop: read state, decide, act, observe, repeat. |
| **Model** | The underlying large language model that powers the agent's decision-making. On Julius: Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT Sol 5.6. |
| **Harness** | The code wrapper around the model that turns it into an agent. Defines the agent loop, the tools the agent can call, the system prompt, the step budget, and how outputs are emitted. On Julius the default harnesses are 'React Toolbelt Agent (250) \- no BUA' and 'React Toolbelt Response api agent (250) \- no BUA'. The '(250)' is the maximum step count. 'no BUA' means browser-use capabilities are disabled. Different harnesses on the same model produce meaningfully different agent behavior. |
| **Platform** | The set of tools available to the agent inside a world. Different platforms expose different toolsets. Julius examples: 'PDF+Filesystem+Code (no MCP, no BUA)', 'PDF+Filesystem+Code+Nextcloud', 'PDF+Filesystem+Code+Nextcloud+BUA'.  The platform is chosen per world based on what tools the agent needs to complete tasks in that domain. |
| **System prompt** | Instructions stored on the harness telling the agent how to behave in general (use tools when needed, complete tasks independently, etc.). Writers do not edit this. It is configured by Studio engineering at the harness level. |
| **User prompt** | The actual task instruction the writer authors and passes to the agent. This is what you write in the Prompt field on a Julius task. |
| **Trajectory** | One complete agent run on one task. Includes the initial messages, every tool call the agent made, every response the model produced, and the final outputs.  |
| **Tool call** | An action the agent took, for example 'read file X', 'run code Y', 'query table Z'. Each tool call shows up as a step in the trajectory. |
| **Step** | One iteration of the agent loop: a single decision, tool call, and observation. The harness step budget caps how many of these the agent gets before it is forced to produce a final answer. |
| **3\. Worlds** |  |
| **World** | A self-contained slice of a simulated professional environment. Contains the documents, data, apps, and tools the agent can interact with. Each world is built for one specific domain and persists across all the tasks created against it. |
| **World files** | The documents (PDF, .docx, .xlsx, .eml, .pptx, etc.) that live in the world's filesystem. Realistic artifacts the agent can read. |
| **World data / world data tables** | Structured data living inside apps within the world, for example records in a Salesforce table, transactions in QuickBooks, employees in ADP. The agent can query these the way a real professional would. |
| **Domain lead** | The expert who owns the spec for an entire domain across all its worlds (all Law worlds, all FP\&A worlds, etc.). Updates instructions as patterns emerge. |
| **Pod** | The team of writers and reviewers attached to one world. Your pod is who you collaborate with day to day. |
| **4\. Tasks** |  |
| **Task** | A prompt, set of annotations, trajectories, gold answer, and rubric representing one unit of work.  The atomic unit Julius produces.  |
| **Prompt (user prompt)** | The instruction text the writer authors that the agent receives. Should read like an challenge/ask from someone in the relevant professional role. |
| **Gold response / golden response / gold output** | The expert-authored correct answer for the task. Writers create this from scratch by doing the task themselves. |
| **Task input files** | Files the writer uploaded specifically for this task, in addition to the world files. The agent can access these the same way it accesses world files. |
| **Rubric** | The collection of criteria (verifiers) on a task. Each verifier is one row of the rubric. |
| **Verifier** | A single rubric criterion attached to a task that defines a specific thing the agent's output must satisfy. Each verifier has criteria text, a difficulty (Low / Medium / High), and an expected file type. Stored as a Studio record (ver\_…). The set of verifiers on a task is the task's grading rubric. |
| **Difficulty** | A field on each verifier (Low / Medium / High). High-difficulty verifiers carry more weight in scoring. |
| **Expected output** | A custom field on each task indicating what kind of deliverable the agent should produce (e.g. 'Make New Doc', 'Edit Existing Doc', 'Make New Sheet', 'Make New Slide Deck'). |
| **Show Your Work** | A custom field where the writer documents their reasoning while building the gold response. Used by reviewers and sometimes by downstream training pipelines. |
| **5\. Task status lifecycle** |  |
| **Drafting Prompt** | Writer is composing the user prompt. |
| **Awaiting Prompt Review** | Writer has finished the prompt and submitted for first-pass review. |
| **In Prompt Review** | A reviewer has picked it up and is evaluating the prompt only (not the gold or rubric yet). |
| **Crafting** | Prompt passed review; writer is building out the golden response and verifiers. |
| **Awaiting Review** | Full task submitted for second-pass review. |
| **In Review** | A reviewer is evaluating the complete task. |
| **Approved** | Task passed both reviews and shipped. |
| **Rejection loop** | Rejection at either review stage loops the task back to the prior writing stage for rework. A task only ships once it clears both reviews. |
| **6\. People and roles** |  |
| **Writer** | Expert who authors tasks: prompt, gold response, verifiers. |
| **Reviewer** | Expert who QAs other writers' tasks at the prompt-review and final-review stages. |
| **Domain lead** | Owns a domain's spec across all its worlds. |
| **EPM (Engagement / Project Manager)** | Mercor staff member running project operations: ramp, throughput, communications. |
| **DRI (Directly Responsible Individual)** | The single person accountable for a given workstream. |
| **Mercor Research** | The internal team that sets the research direction Julius serves. |
| **7\. Process and ops vocabulary** |  |
| **AHT (Average Handling Time)** | How long, on average, a writer or reviewer spends per task. |
| **Insightful** | The time-tracking tool. Use the 'Project Julius \- World Building' timer when world building and 'Project Julius \- Task Writing' when writing tasks. Clock in when you start, clock out when you stop. |
| **Time fraud** | Logging time on Insightful while not actually working. Cause for removal. |
| **Pacing** | The expected weekly volume of completed tasks. Driven by the project's milestone targets. |
| **Office hours** | Daily live sessions for questions and walk-throughs. Times and links live in the master instructions doc. |
| **8\. Acronyms** |  |
| **BUA** | Browser Use Agent |
| **MCP** | Model Context Protocol |
| **AHT** | Average Handling Time |
| **EPM** | Expert Project Manager |
| **DRI** | Directly Responsible Individual |
| **QC** | Quality Control |
| **RLS** | RL Studio (the platform's earlier name; still the Linear team key) |
| **PII** | Personally Identifiable Information |
| **NSFW** | Not Safe For Work (nudity, profanity, etc.) |
| **LLM** | Large Language Model |

# 💾 App Glossary

# App Glossary

## **Current scope**

This glossary is the current production and active testbed scope: 8 general services and 42 domain apps, for 50 services/apps in total.

Use only the apps named in App Configuration for the task. Do not add, remove, or replace an app. If a required app does not start or its data does not load, tell Apps Ops and wait.

## **How interfaces work**

• Normal domain apps use MCP. The agent reads and acts through MCP.  
• A seeded platform may also contain a BUA service only because the CSV loader lives there. That BUA is not an agent interaction surface.  
• Personal/Consumer apps are the exception. Chatwoot, Easy\!Appointments, OpenTripPlanner, and WooCommerce use BUA.  
• FreeCAD and KiCad are no-seed file apps. They use MCP against files included in the world.  
• Loader success is not app proof. For a normal seeded app, confirm the loaded data through the app’s MCP.

## **What App Configuration tells you**

• App name: the exact app to include.  
• Version: the approved app build.  
• Seed or file source: the world data to load or the files to attach.  
• Credentials: only when a Personal/Consumer browser app needs them.

## **Apps by area**

• General services: File system; Email; Calendar; PDF; Word; Excel; PowerPoint; Code execution.  
• Shared: Wiki.js; Nextcloud.  
• Financial services and accounting: ERPNext; QuickBooks; Fineract; OpenInsure; FASLR; Caseware OnPoint; FloQast; FP\&A Forecaster; GoSystem Tax RS; NetSuite; ONESOURCE Tax Provision; Optro; Workiva.  
• Law: DocuSeal; Docassemble.  
• HR and recruiting: BambooHR; SAP SuccessFactors Recruiting; SAP SuccessFactors Onboarding; Workday; Greenhouse.  
• Projects and operations: Atlassian; OpenProject; Odoo; Gitea; NocoDB; CKAN.  
• Personal/Consumer: Chatwoot; Easy\!Appointments; OpenTripPlanner; WooCommerce.  
• Data and analytics: JupyterHub; Metabase; dbt; MySQL; Grafana.  
• Education and research: Canvas; OpenEduCat; Zotero.  
• Engineering: FreeCAD; KiCad.

## **General services**

### File system

Interface: MCP  
What it is: The shared files and folders inside the world.  
What the agent can do: List, search, read, create, rename, move, edit, and delete world files.  
Example task: Find the source files for a report, update the report, and save the result.  
Login: None.

### Email

Interface: MCP  
What it is: The world’s seeded mailbox. This is the standard Mail app, not Gmail.  
What the agent can do: Read messages and threads, search mail, manage drafts, and send mail when the task requires it.  
Example task: Find the latest customer message and draft a reply using the facts in the world.  
Login: None. The mailbox is pre-authenticated.

### Calendar

Interface: MCP  
What it is: The world’s seeded calendar.  
What the agent can do: Read, search, create, update, and delete calendar events.  
Example task: Find an open time and schedule a review meeting.  
Login: None. The calendar is pre-authenticated.

### PDF

Interface: MCP  
What it is: Tools for reading and producing PDF documents.  
What the agent can do: Extract text, inspect pages, combine information, and create a final PDF when requested.  
Example task: Read a policy PDF and produce a short PDF summary.  
Login: None.

### Word, Excel, and PowerPoint

Interface: MCP  
What it is: The three Office document services used for .docx, .xlsx, and .pptx files.  
What the agent can do: Read, create, and update documents, workbooks, and presentations.  
Example task: Update an Excel model, write a Word memo, and prepare a PowerPoint summary.  
Login: None.

### Code execution

Interface: MCP  
What it is: A controlled runtime for scripts and data work inside the world.  
What the agent can do: Run code to inspect data, calculate results, transform files, and support the task.  
Example task: Calculate monthly totals from CSV files and save a checked output.  
Login: None.

## **Domain apps**

### Atlassian

Interface: MCP  
What it is: A combined Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket work system.  
What the agent can do: Manage issues, search and edit wiki pages, and inspect repositories and code.  
Example task: Trace a product issue from its Jira ticket to the related Confluence plan and Bitbucket code.

# **Key Restrictions**

## **Legal Restrictions**

| Do Not Upload Proprietary or Prior Work You may not upload resources that you created for your job or for another project. You may use these documents as inspiration, but do not directly upload any work produced for another purpose. No proprietary information may be uploaded or used within any world or task in this project. |
| :---- |

**Artifacts Found Online**

You will likely be doing research on the internet to populate the world. Download any relevant resources and upload them to the Within World folder. The bullets below cover the categories you must check before using anything you find.

* **Paywalled content**: you can only use files that are publicly available on the internet; anything behind a paywall or login is unacceptable.  
* **Copyrighted content**: carefully review all materials to determine whether they are subject to copyright; anything under copyright is unacceptable.   
* **Licensed content**: do not include any content that requires a paid license, special permission, or restricted use. Only use content that is clearly free for public use.  
* **Attribution requirements**: if content is licensed for reuse with attribution (*e.g.*, Creative Commons), ensure proper attribution is included and documented.  
* **Questions or uncertainty**: if you are unsure whether content is trademarked, licensed, or otherwise restricted, escalate the question to your team lead before uploading.

| Stick to Public or Government Sources Default to resources from a government entity or content that is explicitly in the public domain. When unsure whether something is trademarked, licensed, or otherwise restricted, escalate to your team lead before uploading. |
| :---- |

## **AI Usage in Task Writing**

AI tools are allowed for ideation and drafting (i.e., as “thought partners”). They are very helpful at scaffolding tasks, giving feedback, and understanding trajectory failures.

However, our goal is to push **beyond the frontier of models’ capabilities**. Using AI models is not a substitute for your domain expertise in doing the tasks. 

* You are fully responsible for everything you submit. If it’s wrong, that’s on you—not the AI.  
  * Verify every value, calculation, and piece of logic manually.  
  * All values must be grounded. No made-up facts, no hallucinated details.

🚨In particular, your prompt, Show Your Work files, completion steps, and golden output must be **your own output**. Prompts and golden outputs must be realistic. We do not want everything to be repetitive, generic, or “AI-sounding”. Rewrite everything in your own words.

Ultimately, we trust you to do your work and use your expert judgement. We believe AI tools can help you to be more efficient; but we do not want quality to fall.

AI and External Tool Usage Policy  
Default Mercor policy: you may use an LLM to fix grammar and diction and to lightly refine phrasing, provided that the fundamental ideas and structure remain your own. Do not ask an LLM to rewrite your responses wholesale. You may not use LLMs to evaluate or grade model responses, to write your justifications or explanations, or to predict code behavior or runtime results. Submissions that are evidently produced by artificial intelligence will be identified and flagged. See https://talent.docs.mercor.com/policies/llm-usage

Project-specific exceptions: on Project Julius, running frontier models inside RL Studio trajectories (for example the Gemini, Claude, and GPT model families) is a sanctioned and expected part of the work, since the goal is to prove where these models fail. Personal Pro subscriptions used for the project are reimbursable through the LLM Reimbursement Form, as described in the LLM Purchase Guide. Synthetic, AI-generated world-building materials are expected for fictional companies and places, subject to the rules in the AI-Generated Content Policy below. 

## **AI-Generated Content Policy**

World builders may use AI tools (Claude) to synthetically generate materials for some phases of the project. **Core tasks and golden outputs must be created by yourself.** 

Some world materials may include interview transcripts, survey results, financials for a fake company, and similar artifacts.

* All AI-generated material should be **thoroughly reviewed** to ensure that it is realistic, appropriate for the scenario, and does not violate any rules of the project.  
* Any mention of the AI used within the document produced should be eliminated (no references to ChatGPT-generated docs or similar).  
* You must only AI-generate materials for fictional companies or places. Financials or other company-level data must be for a fictitious company.  
* **You must hand-author every seed entity (core company, key people, and named counterparties) from scratch, and never use AI-generated names verbatim** — recurring defaults like “Meridian,” “Acme Corp,” “TechNova Solutions,” “Globex Corporation,” “Apex Dynamics,” “John Smith,” or “Jane Doe,” or “Vera” create realism issues, obvious AI fingerprints, and repeated overlap across worlds. Banned AI-default names are a hard send-back; the full canonical list (single source of truth, synced with the AutoQC name check) is here: [Banned AI-Default Names List](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TdFs0qDZT234PGJvRX9X4U-18qNeggnLcimx1v8WE1w/edit)  
* Separately, 555-01xx phone numbers are the correct fiction convention (keep them); the realism concern is uniform or round data (identical figures across periods), not the 555 prefix. **Use AI for inspiration, then spend a minute making every name feel natural, unique, and domain-appropriate before you use it.**

| Fictional Entities Only AI-generated financials or other company-level data only for fictitious companies and places. Never AI-generate materials representing a real company or real person. |
| :---- |

| Don't Use AI Names Verbatim AI-generated company, stakeholder, and personnel names should never be used exactly as suggested. Spend a minute making each one feel natural, unique, and appropriate for the domain before it goes into a world. |
| :---- |

## **Banned AI-Default Names**

Mirrors the [canonical Banned AI-Default Names doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TdFs0qDZT234PGJvRX9X4U-18qNeggnLcimx1v8WE1w/edit) (the single source of truth, also referenced by the AutoQC name-presence check wow\_banned\_ai\_default\_names). Edit the canonical doc to change the list everywhere; this section is a copy. Last updated 2026-08-15.

### **How to use**

Hand-author seed names from scratch (core company, key people, named counterparties); never ship a name an AI proposed first. Match case-insensitively on whole-word boundaries. Tier A \= banned: any occurrence is a defect, remove or rename before submit. Tier B \= review: frequent AI defaults that also collide with real words, so flag and sanity-check rather than hard-fail.

### **Tier A — banned (hard-fail)**

**Companies:** Meridian, Acme, Globex, TechNova, Contoso, Cyberdyne, Initech, Vandelay, Umbrella Corporation, Stark Industries, Wayne Enterprises, Hooli, Soylent, Wonka, Pied Piper, Northwind Traders, Oscorp.

**Placeholder people:** John Smith, Jane Doe, John Doe.

Meridian also covers compound forms (Meridian Corp / Inc / Group / Partners / Labs / Systems / Bank / Capital) and meridian.com-style email domains.

### **Tier B — review (flag, not fail)**

Nexus, Apex, Zenith, Vertex, Vantage, Summit, Horizon, Pinnacle, Catalyst, Synergy, Vanguard, Paramount, Keystone, Cornerstone, Beacon, Nimbus, Lumen, Orion, Atlas, Cascade, Sterling, Evergreen, Emerald, Vera, Northwind.

### **555 phone numbers**

555-01xx numbers are the correct fictional convention; keep them. The realism problem is uniform or round data (identical figures across periods) and unfilled placeholder blanks such as 555-555-5555, not the 555 prefix itself.

# 🌍 Phase 1: World Creation Process

# **World Building Primer**

*This guide covers what a world is, how to build one, and how to document its structure in knowledge transfer documents. Work through each section in order.*

## ***⚠️Note**: All experts unless notified in specific internally-based cases in Accounting and Law will be World Builders and will build worlds.*

## **What is a World?**  

A world is a realistic, self-consistent corporate, personal, or organizational digital environment populated with documents, data, applications, and personas that an AI agent navigates to complete tasks. A world is not a single task; it is the environment that supports multiple tasks.

When you build a world, you create a fully realized organization with the kind of messy, interconnected documentation that exists inside real companies. The agent must search through these artifacts, cross-reference information, handle inconsistencies, and synthesize conclusions, just as a human knowledge worker would.

## 

## **What makes a great world?**

* Represents a specific organization (company, hospital, law firm, government agency) with a realistic operational context. Define the industry, size, geography, and other key characteristics.  
* Contains \~**50 artifacts** across multiple modalities  
* Organized in folder hierarchies that mirror real organizational structures. A compliance team files differently than a sales team; your world should reflect this.  
* Information is deliberately scattered. No single document contains everything an agent needs; the agent must discover, navigate, and cross-reference across multiple sources.  
* Contains both File System data as well as Application data.  
* Supports 2-6 tasks that will fail the model  
* Contains defendable “traps” that are intended to make the world taskable and challenging for the agent.

For context, our Auto QC checks for the following dimensions, and more: 

| Realistic Document Texture And Markings File Volume And Format Diversity Supports Independent Tasks No Blind Filesystem Searches Needed No Synthetic Markers Or Placeholder Data Coherence Flag Ratio Anomaly Detection Catch-All No Synthetic Substitutes For Real-World Facts External Citations Resolve To Real Content In-World vs Out-Of-World Separation Timeline And Dates Are Coherent | Personnel Names, Titles, And Roles Are Consistent No Broken Document References Document Chronology Is Causally Consistent Consistent Naming All Numerical Values And Constraints Are Consistent Across The World Voice, Tone, And Formatting Vary By Author And Document Type Traceability And Cohesion Realism Flag Ratio File Integrity Defect Rate  |
| :---- | :---- |

## **Real vs fictional entities** 

* The core entity of your world must be fictional. The central organization your scenario is about (and its people) is invented, and all of its data is synthetic.  
* Real companies may appear as supplementary material, not as the core entity or a central party. When you include a real company, you must use its real, publicly available data: for example, a 10-K, an earnings release, a public statement, or other documents downloaded from the open web.  Never fabricate, alter, or synthesize data for a real company.  
* Match the data to the entity. Fictional entities get synthetic data; real entities get their real public data. Never mix the two: no synthetic numbers on a real company, and no real filings repurposed as your fictional core entity's own records.  
* Do not let a "fictional" name accidentally match a real one.

**How to pick and check a name:**

* Invent a clearly made-up name  
* Search it on the web in quotation marks with the industry word (e.g. "Northwind Components" distributor).  
* If any real company or person with a similar name could be confused for yours, change it. When in doubt, change it.  
* Real public bodies (the IRS, a court, U.S. GAAP) are fine to reference. A real private company is fine only as supplementary material with its real public data, and must never be the core entity or a named central party.

## **How We Measure World Quality**

We measure quality against three north stars: **depth**, **realism**, and **factual integrity**. Each one is the difference between a world that supports a task and a world that supports a real evaluation of agent reasoning.

| Depth Enough material to support 5 complex tasks that current AI models cannot complete correctly. Driven by complexity, interconnectedness, and the number of core files. | Realism Matches the texture, friction, and irregularity of real workplaces. Signals are buried in noise, just like real-life production. See the Traps and Noise table on the next page. | Factual Integrity Every shared fact, figure, and entity is consistent across every artifact in the world unless it is a planned trap. No contradictions across files. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

#### **Depth**

A good world has enough material to support \~5 complex tasks. Complexity,  interconnectedness, traps, and the number of core files are the most important drivers. We recommend \~50 file system artifacts, depending on your domain’s complexity, plus app data. Use your discretion—remember that the world is fixed at the end of the build process and no other files can be added during the task-writing phase. Make sure there's enough substantive content to support lots of varied tasks.

## ***⚠️Note**: A world is FIXED after it is completed and no revisions will be allowed once task writing begins\!*

####  **Artifact types**

Different artifact types serve different purposes. Use the mix below to build depth.

| Type | Format | When to Use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **File System** | Word documents | Internal planning docs, call notes, etc. |
|  | Spreadsheets | Financials, forecasts, data history, reports, and schedules. Must align with real-world professional practices. |
|  | Presentations | Executive decks, meetings, presentations, etc. |
|  | PDFs | Documents, regulatory or publicly available docs, any static content no longer being updated internally. |
| **App** | Application Data | Mock applications that may mimic popular ERPs, CRMs, knowledge bases, or other business tools. Used to test an agent’s ability to retrieve and parse data, transfer information, update fields, change record states, and execute end-to-end software workflows. |

#### **Why World Depth Matters**

The richness of the world directly determines the quality and difficulty of the tasks it can support. A shallow world with a handful of documents produces shallow tasks. 

A deep world with layered dependencies and cross-document references produces the long-horizon, multi-step tasks that genuinely test agentic capabilities.

#### **Realism**

A world is only as useful as its similarity to the real-world context. If it doesn't mimic the texture, friction, and irregularity of how things actually work in the real world, the tasks built on top of it won't reflect real challenges either. Realism is what turns a setting into a stress test: signals buried in noise, etc., are exactly what models and workers must learn to navigate in production.

This fidelity is critical as we train models to perform real-world tasks. In the QC stage, we ensure world realism by identifying:

* Stylistic consistency  
* Any markers of synthetic generation  
* Document texture and more.

## **Traps and Noise** 

In-world noise and/or traps are encouraged when they create realistic reasoning challenges. They are prohibited when they make tasks unsolvable.

| ✅ Allowed/Defendable | ❌ Not allowed  |
| :---- | :---- |
| Embedded rules—only if stated clearly in a findable place (e.g., an email) Sequential, version, or recency-based canonicality Canonicality by seniority of the source Canonicality by explicit statement Canonicality by official doc over email Volume noise: many tables, many records, many files  Company-specific policy or guidance; must be sensible, findable, clearly presented | For example:  Unsolvable tasks, i.e., tasks that rely on information/assumptions not given in the world or prompt Highly subjective matters of taste with no in-world reasoning path Unrealistic, non-findable embedded rules (e.g., a screenshot of a doc in a random folder with an alphanumeric title containing the only missing value) |

**Factual Integrity**  
Factual integrity is the connective tissue of a world. It is the shared facts, figures, and entities that anchor every document to a single underlying reality. When a name, number, or date (referred to as “thresholds”) appears in one artifact, it must hold true everywhere else it surfaces; otherwise, the world stops being one world and becomes a collection of contradictory drafts. This consistency is what makes a world reasoning-worthy: tasks can only test real synthesis and judgment when the underlying facts actually line up across files.

To hold these key factoids consistent across the artifact of the worlds, you will be designated thresholds in your World Specs [(see more details here).](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1XeGXt0L0H6higW4VCICYVqHv2NF9NUrOZFG04YwE1MI/edit?tab=t.s5ppyghdo1p9)

## **Regional Requirements**

The scope of all worlds, tasks, scenarios, and evaluations must be based on **United States jurisdiction, norms, standards, and professional practices**.

Domain-specific content should reflect U.S. frameworks and expectations. Examples include, but are not limited to:

* **Accounting:** U.S. GAAP, U.S. financial reporting standards, and U.S.-based business practices.  
* **Law:** U.S. federal and state legal systems, regulations, case law, and legal procedures.  
* **HR, Finance, and other regulated domains:** U.S. laws, regulations, terminology, and operational practices.  
*  **Engineering:** Two standards tracks. Engineering is the exception to the U.S.-only rule above. Every engineering world is built to exactly one standards track, U.S. or International, declared at the Spec stage and marked in the world name as \[U.S.\] or \[INTL\]. Cite only the codes and use only the unit conventions of that world's track. Do not mix tracks within a world.  
  * U.S. track (U.S. customary units where conventional):  
    * Civil / Structural: IBC, ASCE 7, ACI 318, AISC 360, AASHTO.  
    * Electrical: National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), IEEE and NESC standards, UL listing conventions.  
    * Mechanical: ASME codes and ASHRAE standards.  
  * International track (SI units):  
    * Civil / Structural: Eurocodes (EN 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1997, 1998\) and ISO structural standards (e.g., ISO 2394, ISO 13822).  
    * Electrical: IEC standards (e.g., IEC 60364, 60947, 61439, 61850\) and IEC-aligned national wiring rules.  
    * Mechanical: ISO standards (e.g., ISO 286, ISO 2768, ISO 1101 GPS, ISO 4126\) and ISO/EN building-services standards (e.g., EN 16798, ISO 52000 series) in place of ASHRAE.

Content, references, or examples originating from outside the United States are **not prohibited** and may be incorporated when relevant. However, for all domains except engineering, the center of gravity of each world should remain within the U.S. context. Core tasks, expected solutions, evaluation criteria, assumptions, and domain expertise should be grounded in U.S. requirements and conventions unless the task explicitly calls for international or comparative analysis.

**Law, Accounting, and Engineering Experts**: During onboarding, you must complete the required Google form specifying your specialization(s) and any regional restrictions. 

* [Law Form](https://forms.gle/uQWoWvEoUJv47ra38)  
* [Accounting Form](https://forms.gle/h9z8UxBb2PoxXvhX7)  
* [Engineering Form](https://forms.gle/BsBWra4RujvUFQwE9)

**Most experts who are not well-versed in U.S. jurisdictions, codes, and standards are not eligible to world-build.**  

**HOWEVER,** engineering experts may world-build on either track; International-track engineers are not required to be versed in U.S. codes, but must build only in the track(s) they selected in the Welcome Poll.

If this applies to you, you will instead be placed into an already-built world to [Task Write]().   
Please also notify your Domain Lead of this restriction upon onboarding.

## **Critical Tips Before You Begin**

**Tip 1\. Build Your World in Stages**

Set up a formal structure that tracks every document you create. Start with foundational operational docs, then let the world grow as tasks are written.

**Tip 2\. The World Spec as the Source of Truth**

Use the World Spec as your **central registry**. Your World Spec is the critical document for grounding both you and the AI systems on what the world should contain. Everything in the world, including entities, documents, thresholds, known issues, domain data, and contributor rules, is registered there. Keep your spec as the single source of truth throughout the build.

Your World Spec contains dedicated tabs for the World & Scenario (a snapshot of the world), Canonical Values (numbers that must align across the entire world), Tasks (task concepts for your future world), and Artifacts (all file registry and app data).

**Tip 3\. Don’t Expect Perfection**

Synth generation of world content will inevitably have errors. The synthetically generated initial world is just that: initial. It is a starting point to kick off the process. 

You need to iterate, clean up, and take full ownership over the final delivery of the world's content.

**👉Link to template: [Julius World Spec Template](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1HwszJium5Ns29lN490KMss7ajS1U5CVr/edit?usp=drive_link&ouid=116757728625579568166&rtpof=true&sd=true).**

# **Expectations for World Building**

Before you start, here is what to expect from a world build: how much time it takes, and the quality bar every world has to clear.

## **Time Expectations**

*A first time full world build should take 15 hours for file system only or 23 hours for app-enabled worlds end to end.*

| Phase | Estimated time |
| :---- | :---- |
| Onboarding and Spec creation & revision | 7 hours (includes 3 hours onboarding allowance) |
| World creation / Revision \- File System | 8 hours |
| World creation / Revision  \- App Data | 8 hours |
| Total  File System only worlds App-enabled worlds |  15 hours 23 hours |

## **Quality Expectations**

*Hours are only half the bar. The other half is quality\!*

| ✅ Build to the Highest Quality Every world is built to the highest standard so it holds up on three dimensions: depth, realism, and taskability. A build that is fast but shallow, unrealistic, or hard to write tasks against does not meet the bar. Reminder: the end goal here is to build a world with a corpus of files that can support 5 tasks that the model FAILS to complete. |
| :---- |

# **Expectations for Reviewers**

Thank you for becoming a reviewer for world building in Julius\! Here are the expectations for your crucial role in this process.

## **Time Expectations**

*Keeping reviewer AHT to these expectations is key to project success. Quick reviews help unblock writers, which reduces the time to build a world. They also mean that your experience and domain expertise gets transferred to the most experts, which makes the entire world-building team stronger.*

| Phase | Estimated time |
| :---- | :---- |
| Spec Review | 15 min |
| World Reviews | 30 min |

## **Quality Expectations**

*Time is only half the bar. The other half is quality\!*

| ✅ Accept Only the Worlds that are TASKABLE Your review helps to keep every world grounded on our three core dimensions: depth, realism, and taskability. A build that is fast but shallow, unrealistic, or hard to write tasks against does not meet the bar. We are relying on your domain expertise to augment AutoQC, so that you can highlight specific deficiencies of a spec in your domain\! Reminder: the end goal here is to build a world with a corpus of files that can support 5 tasks that the model FAILS to complete. |
| :---- |

## **Communication Expectations**

*As a key part of the team, communication is key to our success\!*

| ✅ RLS: Keep all comments here\! Please put all comments and feedback in RLS. This keeps all information about a world build in one location. That way, the team can quickly understand what issues AutoQC missed. Also, another reviewer/EPM can assist with reviews if you are unavailable, as they have full context on the task. |
| :---- |
| **✅ RLS: Claim every review\!** Please make sure to claim every review in RLS and send back if revisions are needed, or approve if the builder is good to go to the next stage. These transitions, and the time spent in them, help us understand and improve the world-building process. |
| **✅ RLS: Note any “Coverage Gaps” in AutoQC** If you ‌find mistakes that AutoQC missed, please annotate them in the orange “Coverage Gaps” section under AutoQC feedback.![][image2] |

**FILE REVISION TIPS**  
Use Claude Code for the revisions. Do not attempt to manually revise your file corpus.  
**Batching**: Try to fix as many issues before reuploading to AutoQC. AutoQC is very slow at this stage, so we want to make sure our revisions are substantial before rerunning it  
**Understand AutoQC**: One round of AutoQC is NOT the whole story.  
AUTOQC IS ITERATIVE: One round of AutoQC does not find all the mistakes.  
A good goal is for around 6-10 rounds of AutoQC, which is our average for efficient revisions  
AUTOQC IS NOT ALWAYS COMPREHENSIVE: Check for the same mistake autoqc flagged in other files  
GUIDE THE REVISIONS: Claude makes mistakes. Make sure YOU understand the mistakes that have to be fixed, and guide Claude efficiently  
One by One fixes: Once the skill gives you a list of core issues, go through each BY ITSELF. DO NOT TRY TO ONE SHOT the fixes, telling Claude to "Fix all" or any similar prompting. That will put you in Autoqc hell.

7. NOTE: If you are on round 5+ of AutoQC and have the tokens, you can start a new chat, and move to Opus to help remediate the rest of the fixes.

# **World Building Tips**

As you embark on building a world, begin by thinking about the issues you have encountered in your work life and in your use of artificial intelligence to assist with your everyday workflow.

**WORK IN REVERSE** 

The greatest asset to your world is pre-thought fails. Come up with **10 ideas** that would require multiple files in your work life to get a response. These should be difficult questions that you, as a domain expert, could answer, but **areas where you know a model struggles to reason.**

For example, a frontier LLM may understand finance but not the inner workings of a financial planning and analysis business dealing with government regulation. Think about every time you used an LLM and it failed. Then create ideas for your world files based on that knowledge.

**LOST IN THE MIDDLE**

You may not have complete control over a file that comes out of a synthetic generation pipeline. You do have control over **editing the file**. Take advantage of this. Bury a critical fact somewhere in the middle of a longer document. This forces a model to read the entire document, and it may not be able to retrieve the information.

**CONFLICTING AUTHORITY**

Many businesses have policy documents that may conflict, not because of the timestamp, but because of the business rules or hierarchy. Perhaps the CEO issued a policy that supersedes one within your corpus. Can the model understand?

**TRAPS**

Traps represent **“human messiness.”** In our everyday lives, this occurs when our interns or junior associates make a small mistake. It can occur within email conversations when drafts are exchanged. 

For example, you edit a document and label it “Final.” Your boss reads the document and sends it back a day later, renamed “Final Final.” Which does the model use?

| Failure pattern | One-shot mechanism |
| :---- | :---- |
| **WORK IN REVERSE** | When creating the world, begin with thoughts of what fails the models (in particular, Gemini 3.8 Flash) in your everyday life. Include 30–50 reasoning ideas across multiple files/apps that would likely work. Build these ideas first, and others around them. |
| **LOST IN THE MIDDLE** | Place critical information needed for a reasoning task in the middle of a dense file. This will test retrieval.  |
| **CONTEXT ROT/TOKEN DEGRADATION** | Models suffer from “token degradation.” Force the model to read long documents, and it will lose retention. |
| **CONFLICTING AUTHORITY** | Two grounded sources disagree; precedence is decided by a rule, not by recency. |
| **TRAPS** | The traps represent “human messiness,” and when compounded, the model struggles to understand. Build more traps. |

 

# 🌏 Common Failure Modes by Domain

**![][image1]**  
Project Julius | World Building  
*Instruction Guide*  
---

 

# **Common Failure Modes by Domain**

## **The Main Idea**

### **Designing "Hard" Tasks for AI**

A task isn't "hard" just because it has many steps; modern models handle long, multi-step chains easily. A truly challenging task forces the model to make a difficult judgment call.

To create these "judgment calls," follow these design principles:

* **Hide the Rules:** Place key rules or policies in your "World" files rather than the prompt. If the prompt gives the answer away, the model doesn't need to do any real work.  
* **Create Ambiguity, Then Resolve It:** Include multiple paths to an answer, but ensure only one is correct according to professional standards. A smart generalist might choose the wrong path, but a domain expert will know the right one.

### **Tactics to Test Model Reasoning:**

* **Use Conflicting Sources:** Provide two sources but define one as the authority. The model must discern which file to trust.  
* **Bury Amendments:** Hide an update in an obscure document that overrides an earlier rule.  
* **Require Integration:** Force the model to pull information from three or more files to find the answer. NOTE: Tasks cannot call on 10 or more files\!  
* **Withhold Proprietary Rules:** Company-specific logic (e.g., specific thresholds or tables) should never be in the prompt; it must exist only within the data provided.  
* **Provide Facts, Not Answers:** For professional standards (e.g., accounting or legal rules), provide the raw facts and framework. Do not write the outcome; let the model apply the standard to reach the correct conclusion.

### **The Gold Standard:**

* **Build to one clear answer:** The goal is for all experts to agree on the outcome.  
* **Avoid ambiguity:** If two experts could reasonably disagree, the task is likely too ambiguous, not "hard."  
* **Reconcile your data:** Unless you have explicitly designed a "trap" (an error for the model to catch), all numbers in your "World" must match perfectly.

---

## **Applies to every world**

- The world must support a task that uses **Applications plus at least two World Files.**  
- Every key number should have **one clear answer**: no ranges, no loose ends.  
- A number that appears in more than one place must **match everywhere.**  
- The right answer should show up in **outputs that can be checked.**


---

## **FP\&A**

**Put this in your world:**

- A decision the prompt leaves open but a domain expert would settle only one way.  
- A figure that differs between the app (ERPNext) and a file, so the agent has to pick the right source.  
- A chain of forecasts where one wrong number throws off everything downstream.  
- Don't include a summary file that states the answer—provide only the raw data so the agent has to compute it. 

**Don't do this:** don't add extra steps to make a task "harder." Extra steps make it easier for the model.

**Example of a legitimate model failure:** the agent excluded $18.72M of payroll and used gross capex ($1.8M) instead of net ($1.566M), overstating book cash by about $18.9M.

---

## **Accounting**

**Put this in your world:**

- A transaction near a period boundary, where a world policy decides which period it belongs to.  
- A rule in the world (not the prompt) that fixes which account something goes in.  
- Two sources where one is the authority; for example, a Credit Agreement that defines a term.  
- Place a tempting-but-wrong figure that's legitimate in context (e.g., a contractual rate the governing definition overrides). You can surround the key file with extra real, in-character documents so the agent must pick the right source among legitimate files

**Don't do this:** don't leave a key number unfixed (no single right answer); don't let values fail to reconcile; and don't build a task where a partial catch still gets the right answer.

**Example of a legitimate model failure:** the model used the FY2024 effective tax rate instead of the $406K of actual cash taxes that the Credit Agreement defined.  
**What not to build:** One task had no answer because working capital in/out was never fixed. That's an ambiguous task, not a failure.

---

## **Sales & Marketing**

**Put this in your world:**

- A rule made of stacked parts that must be combined (e.g., discounts that stack).  
- An amendment buried in a less-obvious source that overrides an earlier rule.  
- A term defined in an SOP that controls what the agent should do.

**Don't do this:** don't make a task answerable from one input file. It must use the app plus at least two world files. Avoid app values that can't be checked against the rest of the world, fake "errors" the model can just handle, and bait that claims "X isn't possible."

**Example of a legitimate model failure:** the pricing master says a 3% pre-pay discount stacks on the 18% base, so the right cap is 21%. The model approved 18%.

---

## **Law**

**Put this in your world:**

- A correct, current authority in the world, with an old or default one as bait, so a wrong figure can be verified.  
- Sign-off thresholds, so that when an amount crosses a threshold, a different person has to sign.  
- Linked figures, so one correction has to carry through the whole memo.  
- Include a document that needs only a small, specific fix. The model tends to over-rewrite and add.

**Don't do this:** don't build forks on judgment calls two lawyers could reasonably disagree on; instead, pin the answer to an authority.

**Example of a legitimate model failure:** the model used per-scan BIPA damages instead of distinct applicants (Cothron/Clay), giving the wrong reserve.

---

## **HR**

**Put this in your world:**

- A policy the prompt won't repeat; a cutoff, an accrual cap, or proration.  
- Answers that require combining several files.

**Build note:** keep the canonical HR data in the ERPNext HR modules, not BambooHR.

**Don't do this:** don't build forks on judgment with no rule behind them (e.g., "who to lay off").

**Example of a legitimate model failure:** the model counted ineligible staff toward a referral incentive, which caused errors downstream.

---

## **Engineering**

**Put this in your world:**

**Build note:**

# **Writing a Spec That Passes (Start Here)**

You write the spec. The pipeline (the automated system that builds your world) reads it and generates the whole world from it. It only has what you wrote and cannot ask you questions, so the spec must be complete and exact. Anything you leave vague, it has to guess.

We have a Claude skill to use to help you fill out the spec, pass Autoqc, and one-shot your spec submission. To use it:

1. Download the skill and template from here: [World Spec Helper V5.2 (AI Skill)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1_Gc-_9hyUM1cqymfAzaLvomYKV473D8U?usp=drive_link)  
2. Put both in a new Claude chat. Cowork with Opus 5 works great.  
3. Tell it you need to fill out the spec template attached, and it will walk you through all the steps\!

Work the [template's]() tabs from left to right.

Use THIS tool to help you include “Apps” in your 10 task ideas\!

## **A few words you will see throughout**

| Word | Plain meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| The pipeline | The automated system that builds the world from your spec. Not a person. |
| Worldbuilder | You. You write the spec and own the world through to the finished files. |
| Canonical value | The one official version of a number, name, or date. When two places disagree, this is the one they must match. |
| Threshold | Another word for a canonical value: a value that must read the same everywhere it appears. |
| Grounding fact | A fact that is simply true and must hold everywhere. |
| Trap | An inconsistency you put in the world on purpose, registered with a Key. |
| Reconcile | The numbers agree and add up. |
| AutoQC | The automated reviewer that scores your spec before a person reviews it. |

## **The Golden Rule**

| App data is the source of truth. Pick each real value once, register it as a Fact with a Key, and make every file and app row carry that same value. If two things differ on purpose, label it a Trap. |
| :---- |

In plain steps: pick the number once → write it on the **Canonical Values** tab → make every file and app row match it → if two things differ on purpose, that is a Trap and you must label it both as a trap in **Canonical Values** and under Trap Content in the  **④ Artifacts** tab. An unlabeled difference reads as a mistake.

## **A worked example: meet Dana**

Dana is a CFO building an Accounting world about a year-end financial review. Watch how Dana fills the World Spec tabs in order.

**World & Scenario.** Dana ticks **ERPNext** (the accounting records live there), which auto-fills the App registry. Then the company snapshot:

* **Bad:** "A mid-size company that sells products."  
* **Good:** "Northwind Components Inc., a U.S. industrial parts distributor, 220 employees, three U.S. warehouses, $43.2M FY2024 revenue. External entities: top 8 customers, two banks, one audit firm."

Dana writes the revenue as exactly **$43.2M** here because that is the value the fact will carry everywhere. Then Dana names every person the scenario needs (CFO, controller, auditor) in the Key Parties and Roles cell so no one shows up later in a file without being introduced here.

**Canonical Values.** Dana registers the headline number and a planned trap:

| Value Name | Type | Value |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| FY2024 revenue (audited) | Grounding fact | $43.2M (sum of ERPNext Sales Invoices) |
| Q4 FY2024 revenue | Grounding fact | $12.1M (part of the $43.2M annual total) |
| Q3 deck vs invoices | Trap | Q3 deck shows $11.0M but invoices sum to $10.4M; intentional; app data wins |

The quarter figure (Q4 FY2024 revenue) must fit inside the annual figure (FY2024 revenue (audited)): the four quarters total the year. The trap names both numbers, says it is intentional, and says which side wins.

**Tasks.** Dana sketches the tasks the world should support, and what registered files, data, and app data are required for the tasks. She lays out 10 distinct and unique tasks to prove the world can carry 5 hard tasks when complete.

**Artifacts.** Dana writes each file row so the pipeline can build it without any questions. This does NOT include app data. The model row:

| Column | Dana's entry |
| :---- | :---- |
| Type | File |
| Name | FY2024 Board Pre-Read |
| Format/App | PPTX |
| Location | /Finance/Board/FY2024\_preread.pptx |
| Label | Key |
| Prepared by/Source | Finance team (CFO office) |
| Description / What to generate | 8-slide board deck summarizing FY2024; slide 2 cites a $43.8M flash revenue estimate. |
| Relates to (IDs) | A07, A12 |
| Trap Content | Stale $43.8M flash figure never refreshed after the audited close — an authentic copy-forward. |
| Tasks | T1 |
| Reference Doc (title only) | Board Deck \- Coca Cola |

## **The rules that matter most**

### Specific files

Every file row must let the pipeline build the file without guessing. The reviewer reads your "Description / What to generate" and other columns; if they do not name the actual sections, figures, or other data, the file cannot be built reliably.

Fill in this sentence for each file:

| `This is a [file type] written by [author]. It contains [the specific sections, slides, metrics, or figures], and its numbers tie to [which Facts].` |
| :---- |

* **Bad:** a 12-slide board deck whose purpose reads only "Prior-period board pack for comparatives."  
* **Good:** "12-slide year-end board deck; one slide per quarter; charts reconcile to FY2024 revenue (audited); opens with the headline number."

### Consistent values (Thresholds)

Every value that appears more than once must read identically everywhere, and every calculated value must equal its inputs. Two ways this breaks:

* **The same number, written two ways.** Bad: prepaid insurance is $90,000 on one tab and $45,000 in the canonical fact. Good: register it once (say $45,000) and match it everywhere via its Key.  
* **A calculated number that does not equal its inputs.** Bad: a row states a bundle is "$936,120 (36 x $26,040)" but 36 x $26,040 \= $937,440. Good: fix the math, or, if the mismatch is intentional, register it as a Trap and say which source wins.

Before you submit, for every calculated number confirm the inputs produce it, and confirm any deliberate difference is a labeled Trap.

### Defendable traps

A good trap has an in-world path the expert can follow to the right answer. Allowed: a newer or higher-version document wins over an older one; a more senior person's word wins over a junior one; an official document wins over an email; a clearly stated, findable rule settles the conflict; volume noise (many records and files).

Not allowed: anything that makes the task unsolvable; a matter of taste with no in-world reasoning path; a needed value hidden where no one would find it. For every trap, trace it end to end from question to answer using only artifacts in the world. If you cannot, add the artifact that resolves it or drop the trap.

### Domain authenticity and depth

* Keep the world's center of gravity in **U.S. jurisdiction** (U.S. GAAP for Accounting, U.S. federal and state law for Law, U.S. regulations for HR and Finance). Use non-U.S. content only where it is genuinely relevant.  
* Aim for\~ **50 file artifacts plus app data**, enough to support 5 hard tasks. The world is **fixed once finished**; nothing can be added later, so build deep now.

### Keep it clean

No author notes, no placeholders, no "TBD" anywhere in the world content. The content should read like what a real U.S. professional in the field would actually produce.

## **Use the AI drafting partner**

The guide gives you an AI assistant as a drafting partner. Attach the template, let it interview you tab by tab, and let your expertise lead: push back on anything generic or wrong before you accept it. Before you submit, ask it to:

* List every value that appears in more than one place and confirm they match.  
* Read every file row and flag any row the pipeline could not build from the Context and Other details alone.  
* List every company and person named as a party and flag any that might match a real one.  
* Trace each trap  
*  from question to answer using only the artifacts you registered.

Fix what it surfaces, then read its work yourself. It can be wrong; you make the final call.

## **Reference / Anchor Files**

Give the pipeline a real-world example of each primary artifact you register. This should be between 10–15. These are genuine documents from the internet that play the same role as one of your artifacts, such as a pitch deck, an employee roster, or a contract. The synthetic file generation pipeline reads these as inputs and copies their look and feel, so it isn’t guessing at what a real version of that artifact should look like. For each reference file, do two things:

1. **Name it in the spec.** Paste the title of the file you downloaded next to the artifact it corresponds to, so the pipeline knows which artifact this example anchors.  
   ![][image28]  
2. **Provide the file itself.** Upload the actual document you downloaded alongside your spec, so the pipeline has the real example to read as an input.

![][image29]

Not every file-system artifact needs an anchor file—but for your most important, primary artifacts, providing one is strongly encouraged; it is the surest way to keep the world realistic. **Anchor files are for the file system only, and are never required for app data.**

## **How approval works, and what happens next**

When your spec is ready, upload it under the “Spec Creation” tab where it says “World Spec Document Upload.” Then select **Run Spec AutoQC** under “Actions” on your World of Worlds task. It runs, moves to **Spec AutoQC Review**, and you make revisions until you pass AutoQC, or have labeled all AutoQC elements you disagree with. Then, you **Submit Spec for Review**. A reviewer then either sends it back (**Needs Spec Fixes**) or approves it: **Approve Spec / Start File System Pipeline**, which kicks off the build. From there you shepherd the world through these stages on the task:

1. **File System:** the pipeline generates the documents → you fix them → **Run File System AutoQC** until it passes → **Approve File System / Start App Data Pipeline**.  
2. **App Data:** the pipeline generates the CSV tables from your fixed files → you fix them → **Run App Data AutoQC** until it passes. Then you communicate to the world building team on Slack that the world needs app data schema and playground check. When they are done → **Approve Verification / Start Knowledge Transfer**.  
3. **Knowledge Transfer:** document the finished world so a task writer can pick it up → **Submit for SPL Sign-off**.  
4. **SPL Sign-off:** a domain lead does the final review and the world goes live. (They can send it back to any stage to fix.)

Each later stage has its own checklist on the **Checklists** tab. Remember: the file data and app data are **hand-corrected after they are generated**, not regenerated.

## **Spec pre-submit checklist**

Tick every box before you Run Spec AutoQC. This is the detailed self-check; the Checklists tab holds the official Spec checklist.

**Golden rule and facts**

- [ ] Every value used in more than one place is on the Canonical Values tab.  
- [ ] Every file and app row that uses a fact has that fact listed in the Description column.  
- [ ] Every calculated number equals its own inputs.  
- [ ] Any quarter or part figures add up to their annual or total figure.  
- [ ] Every on-purpose difference is labeled Type \= "Trap," naming both values and which side wins.  
- [ ] Every trap is solvable: I traced a path from question to answer using only in-world artifacts.

**Files**

- [ ] Every File row could be built by the pipeline with zero questions asked.  
- [ ] "Description / What to generate" names actual sections, metrics, and figures.  
- [ ] Every File row's Description matches the facts the file really cites.  
- [ ] File types, sizes, and lengths are believable.  
- [ ] The world has \~50 artifacts total, enough for \~5 hard tasks.

**Apps**

- [ ] Only the apps actually used are ticked on the World Context tab.  
- [ ] Each app row's "What to generate" has real volumes, specifics, and constraints.  
- [ ] App values match the grounding facts exactly.  
- [ ] Every app row that carries a trap has it listed in Trap Content.  
- [ ] Make sure that only apps included in the world are referenced

**Real vs fictional / synthetic data**

- [ ] The core entity is fictional and its data is fully synthetic; no real company or person is the core entity or a central party.  
- [ ] Any real company appears only as supplementary material and uses its real, publicly available data (for example, 10-Ks, filings, or public statements); no synthetic data is attached to a real company.  
- [ ] Every fictional company and person name has been web-checked and does not match a real one.

**People, dates, and cleanliness**

- [ ] Every person the scenario needs is listed on the World Context tab.  
- [ ] No dates or time periods contradict each other.  
- [ ] No author notes, placeholders, or "TBD" anywhere in the content.  
- [ ] Content reads like what a real U.S. professional in this field would produce.  
- [ ] Every tab is completed; no grey REF tab or blue computed cell was edited.  
- [ ] No apps were referenced or included for a filesystem-only world  
- [ ] For a world with \>10 employees, a roster has been created.

**Final pass with the AI drafting partner**

- [ ] I asked it to confirm that the cross-artifact values match.  
- [ ] I asked it to flag vague file rows and fixed them.  
- [ ] I asked it to flag any real company used as the core entity, or real-company data that was synthesized rather than sourced, plus mismatched Facts, and fixed them.  
- [ ] I asked it to trace each trap to its answer and fixed any it could not solve.
